Family Health

What an endometrial thickness result means

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An ultrasound measurement of the uterine lining can look worrying without an explanation. There is no single normal thickness for everyone: cycle timing, life stage, medicines, symptoms and the appearance of the tissue all help determine what it means.

The endometrial stripe is a description, not a diagnosis

The endometrium is the lining inside the uterus. An imaging report may call its visible outline the endometrial stripe or endometrial echo and give a thickness in millimetres. This is a measurement of normal anatomy, not the name of a disease. Its significance depends on the scan, symptoms and stage of life.

The lining does not always appear as one dark line. Ultrasound brightness and layering change through the cycle, and MRI uses different image signals. Endometriosis is a separate condition involving tissue similar to the uterine lining outside the uterus; measuring the stripe alone neither diagnoses nor excludes it.

How the lining changes during a menstrual cycle

During menstruation, part of the lining is shed. It is generally thin just afterwards, then grows during the proliferative phase under the influence of oestrogen. Near ovulation, an ultrasound may show a layered or three-line appearance. The proliferative phase leads up to ovulation rather than beginning only at the end of the cycle.

After ovulation, progesterone changes the lining during the secretory phase. It often becomes thicker and more uniformly bright on ultrasound as it prepares for possible implantation. If pregnancy does not occur, hormone levels fall and another period follows. These ordinary changes explain why measurements from different cycle days may differ.

Typical cycle measurements are not universal cutoffs

Illustrative descriptions often place the lining at a few millimetres around menstruation, roughly five to seven millimetres in the early proliferative phase, up to about eleven near ovulation and sometimes around sixteen in the secretory phase. Published ranges overlap and differ with imaging technique, cycle pattern and the population studied.

Do not use those numbers as a pass–fail chart. A result cannot be labelled healthy, infertile or cancerous just because it falls above or below a quoted average. Before menopause, no single thickness threshold reliably settles every case of abnormal bleeding. Hormonal contraception, fertility treatment and irregular ovulation can also change the expected pattern.

Before puberty, adult cycle rules do not apply

Before puberty, the uterine lining is usually thin and may be difficult to see clearly. It does not normally follow the same monthly pattern as a regularly menstruating adult. Age, hormonal development and the reason for imaging matter when interpreting a child’s scan.

An adult reference chart should not be used to reassure or diagnose a child. Unexpected vaginal bleeding or signs of unusually early puberty need a paediatric assessment. The clinician can decide whether the finding reflects normal developmental context, hormone exposure or a problem that needs investigation.

Early pregnancy needs more than a thickness measurement

The endometrium changes to support implantation, and early-pregnancy imaging eventually identifies structures such as the gestational sac. A thickened lining alone cannot confirm a pregnancy, establish where it is located or show that it is developing normally. There is no universal two-millimetre stripe threshold that diagnoses a healthy early pregnancy.

When pregnancy is possible, assessment may include a pregnancy test, appropriately timed ultrasound and sometimes repeat blood tests or scans. Pain, bleeding, dizziness or shoulder-tip pain can require urgent assessment for ectopic pregnancy or another problem. Do not let a report describing a thick lining delay care or substitute for locating the pregnancy.

After birth, the scan has a different context

The uterus and its cavity change substantially in the weeks after delivery. Blood, fluid and shed tissue may be visible, and a thicker-looking lining or material in the cavity can occur during normal recovery. These appearances alone do not prove that placental tissue has been retained or that a procedure is required.

The timing after birth, bleeding, pain, fever, ultrasound appearance and sometimes blood-flow findings must be considered together. A single percentage from a postpartum study cannot be applied to all pregnancies or interpreted as a rate of retained placenta. Heavy or increasing bleeding, fever, worsening pain or feeling faint needs prompt maternity assessment. The return of cyclical changes varies, particularly with breastfeeding.

Bleeding after menopause must be assessed

After menopause, the lining usually becomes thinner because hormone stimulation has changed. Any new vaginal bleeding after twelve months without a natural period needs medical assessment, even a single small episode. Thin tissue and benign polyps are possible causes, but symptoms should not be dismissed as an ordinary return of periods.

A measurement of four millimetres or less has historically been used to help triage postmenopausal bleeding. In April 2026, ACOG updated its US guidance to recommend ultrasound together with endometrial tissue sampling for most patients at the initial assessment. A thin measurement is not a universal reason to omit a biopsy. Follow the current local pathway and the clinician’s assessment.

An incidental thicker lining is a different situation

A thickness found on a scan in someone without bleeding is not interpreted in the same way as a finding in someone with postmenopausal bleeding. Being above four millimetres does not itself mean cancer. The overall appearance, whether the lining was fully seen, medicines and personal risk factors influence whether further assessment is appropriate.

Do not ignore a flagged finding, but do not assume that every asymptomatic measurement requires the same procedure. Ask the ordering clinician to explain the reason for follow-up. Routine ultrasound screening is not recommended for every symptom-free person at average risk, and a Pap test does not screen the uterine lining for endometrial cancer.

Polyps can create a focal thickened area

An endometrial polyp is a growth arising from the uterine lining. It may produce a localized area that looks thick or irregular, sometimes with bleeding between periods or after menopause. Many polyps are benign, but imaging cannot always determine the nature of every growth.

The decision to observe, investigate further or remove a polyp depends on symptoms, age, risk factors and its appearance. Hysteroscopy can allow a clinician to look inside the cavity and obtain or remove tissue when indicated. A focal finding deserves its own interpretation rather than being reduced to the average thickness of the whole lining.

Fibroids arise from the uterine muscle

Fibroids are common, usually benign growths of the uterine muscle. A fibroid near or projecting into the cavity can distort the lining and contribute to heavy bleeding. It is not the same tissue process as an overgrowth of endometrial glands.

Location and size matter more than a single prevalence statistic. Some fibroids make the stripe difficult to measure accurately. The clinician may consider additional imaging or a cavity examination if the original scan cannot explain symptoms. Not every fibroid needs treatment, and the right approach depends on bleeding, discomfort and reproductive plans.

Tamoxifen and other hormones change interpretation

Tamoxifen is used to treat or reduce the risk of certain breast cancers. It can have oestrogen-like effects on the uterine lining, including changes associated with polyps or thickening, and can increase endometrial-cancer risk in some groups, particularly after menopause. It does not simply cause one predictable thickness or prove that menopause has occurred.

Report unexpected bleeding while taking it. Ultrasound thickness can be less specific in this setting, and routine scanning without symptoms has not proved a useful universal screening strategy. Do not stop tamoxifen yourself: decisions should involve the oncology and gynaecology teams. Mention hormone replacement therapy and contraception too, because the regimen affects the expected appearance and bleeding pattern.

Hyperplasia requires assessment of the tissue

Endometrial hyperplasia means excessive growth of glands in the lining. It is often related to prolonged oestrogen stimulation without enough progesterone, including situations where ovulation is infrequent. It can occur around menopause or earlier in life. A thick scan can raise suspicion, but a tissue sample is needed to establish the diagnosis and type.

Hyperplasia without atypia and atypical hyperplasia, also called endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia in a commonly used system, have different risks and management. Some findings can be managed with progestogen treatment and surveillance, while others need more extensive treatment. Fertility goals matter, but a thickness number alone should not determine a medication or operation.

Cancer is one possible cause, not the meaning of “thick”

Endometrial cancer starts in the lining of the uterus. Abnormal bleeding is an important symptom, especially after menopause. Persistent irregular bleeding, unusual discharge or pelvic symptoms can also need investigation. Many people with these symptoms have a noncancerous cause, but the cause should be established rather than guessed.

Neither a thick nor a thin measurement can answer every cancer question. Persistent or recurrent bleeding needs reassessment even after an initially reassuring scan or sample. If tissue is insufficient or a focal lesion is suspected, the clinician may recommend another sampling approach or hysteroscopy. A result should always be interpreted with the clinical history.

A thin lining can be normal or reflect low oestrogen

A thin lining is expected at some times, including soon after menstruation and commonly after menopause. Hormonal contraception may also keep it thin. Endometrial atrophy describes thinning associated with reduced stimulation; fragile tissue can sometimes contribute to bleeding, but that diagnosis should not be assumed without evaluating the symptom.

There is no need to try to thicken every thin lining with supplements or hormones. In fertility care, the meaning depends on treatment stage and the wider assessment, and a single scan is not a definitive fertility test. Ask what the measurement changes in your particular plan before starting a product advertised to improve implantation.

Low oestrogen before menopause has several possible causes

Periods may become infrequent or stop when the hormonal signals supporting ovulation are disrupted. Low energy availability, restrictive eating, intense exercise or substantial stress can contribute to hypothalamic amenorrhoea. Ovarian insufficiency and other hormone conditions are different possibilities; some cases of ovarian insufficiency are associated with autoimmune disease.

A thin stripe does not diagnose any of these conditions on its own. Pregnancy should be considered when periods stop, and assessment may involve history, examination and selected hormone tests. Treatment addresses the cause, including nutrition and broader health where relevant, rather than focusing only on changing the ultrasound number.

Symptoms matter whatever the measurement shows

Arrange assessment for bleeding between periods, unusually heavy or frequent bleeding, periods that become widely spaced or stop unexpectedly, persistent pelvic pain, painful sex or difficulty conceiving. Cycle patterns vary with age, postpartum recovery and medicines, so a rigid cycle-length rule is not sufficient. Symptoms are not a reliable way to classify the lining as too thick or too thin.

Seek urgent help for very heavy bleeding, faintness, severe or worsening pain, or possible pregnancy with concerning symptoms. After menopause, even light new spotting needs assessment. You do not need to wait for an annual check or for a second scan to confirm a change before reporting a problem.

Ask what the report means for your next step

Bring the date of your last period, the bleeding pattern, medicines, pregnancy possibility and any previous reports. Ask whether the lining was completely visible, whether the finding was uniform or focal, and whether cycle timing could explain it. If a repeat scan is advised, ask when and what question it is intended to answer.

The next step may be observation, a timed repeat scan, biopsy, hysteroscopy or another investigation. Agree on how results will be communicated and what to do if symptoms continue. The aim is a clear explanation and an appropriate plan, not achieving one ideal millimetre measurement for every stage of life.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Interpret thickness with symptoms, menstrual or menopausal status, medicines and whether the lining was adequately visualized.

Current April 2026 ACOG guidance recommends ultrasound plus tissue sampling for most initial postmenopausal-bleeding assessments; do not rely on an older thin-stripe rule alone.

How BeMama can help

Keep the report with your bleeding dates and medicine list, and ask for the next step in clear language.

When to seek help

New bleeding after menopause needs assessment. Severe pain, very heavy bleeding, faintness or possible pregnancy with concerning symptoms needs urgent help. Do not stop tamoxifen or start hormones without advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The endometrial stripe describes anatomy, not a diagnosis.
  • Normal cyclic variation prevents one universal premenopausal thickness cutoff.
  • A thick lining does not automatically mean cancer, and a thin lining does not dismiss persistent bleeding.
  • Pregnancy, postpartum recovery, tamoxifen and menopausal status need separate interpretation.

Frequently asked questions

Does “endometrial stripe” mean something is wrong?

No. It is an imaging description of the lining inside the uterus. The measurement needs to be interpreted in context.

Is sixteen millimetres always abnormal before menopause?

No. Thickness varies through the cycle, and a thicker secretory-phase lining can be physiological. Symptoms, appearance, cycle timing and risk factors guide the assessment.

Can a two-millimetre lining confirm early pregnancy?

No thickness measurement can confirm location or viability of a pregnancy. Testing and appropriately timed imaging are needed for the clinical question.

Does material in the uterus after birth always mean retained placenta?

No. Blood and normal recovery changes can produce similar appearances. Symptoms and the full ultrasound assessment determine whether retained tissue is suspected.

Does more than four millimetres after menopause mean cancer?

No. It is not a diagnosis. Bleeding, the full scan appearance, medicines and individual risk determine the next step.

Can a thin lining rule out cancer when I have postmenopausal bleeding?

Not on its own. Current ACOG guidance favours ultrasound plus sampling for most initial assessments. Persistent or recurrent bleeding needs reassessment regardless of thickness.

Should everyone without symptoms have ultrasound screening?

No. Routine screening is not recommended for every symptom-free person at average risk. A clinician should interpret an incidental finding individually.

Should I stop tamoxifen if the lining looks thick?

Do not stop it yourself. Report abnormal bleeding and discuss the finding with the gynaecology and oncology teams.

Does a thin stripe mean I cannot become pregnant?

A single measurement is not a complete fertility assessment. Its significance depends on cycle or treatment stage and other findings.

Which symptoms should I report?

Report new postmenopausal bleeding, persistent irregular or heavy periods, pelvic pain, painful sex or unexpected loss of periods. Severe pain, heavy bleeding with faintness or possible pregnancy with concerning symptoms needs urgent care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
